clue.text: Cup dispensers I dry, once unwrapped and clean…

indicators.note: a thing unwrapped has lost its outer covering, so only the inside of the word is kept

blocks.note: the Football Association hands out the FA Cup
taken as written
the middle letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone drying the cups after washing up, leading into the next clue with an ellipsis.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cup dispensers' suggests a kitchen gadget, but it is the body that awards a football trophy, the FA. The ellipsis just links the surface to 3 across.
explanation.definitionFit: Fair play is clean play, so both words describe honest conduct that keeps within the rules.

clue.text: Extract from Beowulf, a bleak myth

indicators.note: an extract is a short passage lifted out of a longer text, so the letters are taken from inside the words

blocks.note: the run of letters spanning the end of the poem's name, the article and the start of the adjective

explanation.surface: A quotation from the Old English epic, described as a grim legend.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across Beowulf, a and bleak.
explanation.definitionFit: A fable is a traditional story, often with talking animals or a moral, so it is close kin to a myth.

clue.text: I see upside-down grebe that has a large bottom

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase for a noun

indicators.note: in a down entry, turning something upside down makes it read from bottom to top

blocks.note: the two words said together make the sound of frozen water
a diving waterbird

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher spotting a diving bird bottom-up as it feeds, with a big rear end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I see' is spoken, giving ICE, and the grebe is turned over to read EBERG. The definition jokes that most of the mass is hidden below the waterline.
explanation.definitionFit: Roughly nine tenths of a floating mass of ice lies underwater, so its submerged base is huge.

clue.text: …start to hurl cups around contemporary-era shelter

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept
turning around faces the other way, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: opening letter
a bra is the garment made of cups
the present era is OUR AGE

explanation.surface: Continuing 1 across, someone throwing cups about in a modern refuge.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cups' stands for the undergarment with cups, which is turned round; 'contemporary era' is the time we live in, our age.
explanation.definitionFit: A harbourage is a place of refuge, originally a harbour for ships, hence any shelter.

clue.text: Outrage relating to the Pope’s pages getting stuck together

indicators.note: the two page abbreviations are shifted so that they sit side by side, which reorders the word

blocks.note: the adjective for things belonging to a pope

explanation.surface: Scandal over a Vatican document whose leaves have glued together.
explanation.walkthrough: P is the abbreviation for page; in the papal adjective the two Ps are apart, and joining them gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To appal someone is to shock and horrify them, which is what outrage does as a verb.

clue.text: One leaving leggy model with signs for summer parties

indicators.note: something that leaves goes away, so that letter is taken out

blocks.note: the Roman numeral for one
the long-legged fashion doll made by Mattel
cues are signals to act or speak

explanation.surface: A tall model leaves a party scene, gesturing towards summer get-togethers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Model' suggests a catwalk, but it is the famous doll; drop its I and add the signals.
explanation.definitionFit: Barbecues are outdoor gatherings where food is grilled, typical social events of warm weather.

clue.text: Detach dried trousers, perhaps, and amputate leg?

blocks.note: first meaning: remove the clips holding washing on a line
second meaning, playful: take away a wooden leg

explanation.walkthrough: A clothes peg holds trousers on the line; a peg leg is a wooden leg, so removing it undoes the peg. The question mark flags the whimsy.
explanation.definitionFit: Taking out clothes clips releases laundry, and a peg is also slang for a wooden leg.

clue.text: Leader from medieval Spain’s conquering force within continent — this one?

definitions.text: Leader from medieval Spain’s conquering force within continent — this one?
definitions.note: the whole clue is the definition

indicators.note: the leader of a word is its first letter, so just that is kept
conquerors overthrow and take the place of the defeated, so one set of letters ousts another

blocks.note: opening letter
E is Spain's international vehicle code, from España
F is the physics symbol for force
a continent south of Europe

explanation.surface: Asking which continent Spain conquered after its medieval era.
explanation.walkthrough: Inside the African continent, ME conquers and replaces F. Read as a whole, the clue points to the continent Spain overran.
explanation.definitionFit: Spanish conquistadors subdued much of the New World, so this landmass fits a continent taken by Spanish force.

clue.text: Naked men get shy dancing and initially perform with make-up

indicators.note: naked means stripped of clothing, so the outer letters are removed and the middle kept
dancers move about, so these letters are jumbled
initially means at the start, so only an opening letter is used

blocks.note: the middle letter
the middle letter
taken as written
the opening letter
to do a play or a song is to perform it
W is a standard abbreviation for with

explanation.surface: Nervous male strippers put on cosmetics before their show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Naked' strips both men and get to their centres; those two Es join shy in the mix, then come A, DO and W.
explanation.definitionFit: Eyeshadow is a cosmetic applied to the eyelids, one kind of facial cosmetic.

clue.text: Party bound by lease?

definitions.note: the whole clue is the definition

indicators.note: something bound by a thing is tied up inside it, so one piece is enclosed

blocks.note: a side is one party in a dispute or contract
to rent a property is to lease it

explanation.surface: A legal question about who is tied to a tenancy agreement.
explanation.walkthrough: Both readings of the whole clue point the same way: the side enclosed by the rent, and a person held to a tenancy.
explanation.definitionFit: A tenant who lives in a property is one of the parties a rental agreement commits to its terms.

clue.text: One who likes Queen but is wary of Sting?

definitions.text: One who likes Queen but is wary of Sting?

blocks.clueFragment: One who likes Queen but is wary of Sting?
blocks.note: surface reading: a music fan who loves the band Queen but not the singer Sting
setter's reading: the ruling female of a hive
setter's reading: the painful jab from an insect

explanation.walkthrough: The capitals make Queen and Sting look like rock acts; lowered, they are the hive's ruler and the insect's weapon, which a person tending hives values and avoids.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who keeps hives prizes a healthy egg-laying female and wears protective gear against painful jabs.

clue.text: Song, perhaps ‘The Sound of Silence’

indicators.note: the sound of a word is how it is spoken, so its pronunciation is wanted

blocks.note: silence is peace and quiet

explanation.surface: Naming the Simon and Garfunkel hit as an example of a song.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make it a song title, but the words split as an indicator plus a synonym for quiet, said aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: A musical piece is any composition, and a song is one example of such a work.

clue.text: Visionary priest’s frightened outburst about Zadok’s initial, corrupt lie

indicators.note: an initial is the first letter of a name, so only that is kept
to be about something is to surround it, so one piece goes round another
corrupted text has its letters spoilt and scrambled

blocks.note: the cry of someone startled
first letter
taken as written

explanation.surface: A seer-priest yelps in fright at a crooked falsehood told by Zadok, another biblical priest.
explanation.walkthrough: Zadok was a priest under King David, which helps the biblical picture; only his first letter is used, inside the yelp.
explanation.definitionFit: Ezekiel was an Old Testament prophet of priestly family, famous for his visions such as the valley of dry bones.

clue.text: Move shingle from these shores?

indicators.note: moving things shifts them about into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written: pebbles on a beach

explanation.surface: Shifting beach pebbles away from the coastline.
explanation.walkthrough: 'From these shores' sounds like the source of the stones, but it is the definition, written from a British setter's point of view.
explanation.definitionFit: For a setter writing in a London newspaper, people or things native to this island country are described with this adjective.

clue.text: A gal swimming close to me weed in the sea

indicators.note: swimming things move about, so these letters are mixed up
the close of a word is its end, so its last letter is taken

blocks.note: taken as written
final letter

explanation.surface: A woman swims near the speaker through seaweed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close to' reads as 'near' in the surface, but it selects the end of the following word.
explanation.definitionFit: Seaweeds are large marine plantlike organisms classed among these simple photosynthetic organisms.

clue.text: Gorilla tossing bottles at another zoo animal?

indicators.note: tossing things throws them about, so their order is jumbled
to bottle something is to hold it inside, so one piece is enclosed

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: An ape in a zoo hurls bottles at a neighbouring enclosure's creature.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottles' looks like a noun being thrown, but it is a verb meaning holds in.
explanation.definitionFit: This large reptile is kept in zoos, like the ape named in the clue, so it is a second captive beast.

clue.text: Tesla getting behind funny guy that’s likely to win

blocks.note: T is the SI symbol for the tesla, the unit of magnetic flux density
the rump is the backside
a card is a comical person

explanation.surface: Elon Musk's car company backing a comedian who looks set to win, with a political wink.
explanation.walkthrough: Tesla suggests the car maker, but it is the scientific unit; 'behind' looks like a position word but is a noun for the buttocks.
explanation.definitionFit: A card from the suit that beats all others, and by extension any decisive advantage, is what tends to secure victory.

clue.text: Entertainer hit on horny northerner ‘out on the pull’ on Christmas Eve

blocks.note: a tap is a light blow

blocks.clueFragment: horny northerner ‘out on the pull’ on Christmas Eve
blocks.note: one of Santa's reindeer, an antlered Arctic creature that pulls the sleigh on the night before Christmas

explanation.surface: A performer makes a pass at a randy man from the north out looking for romance at Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Horny' and 'on the pull' suggest a flirt, but they mean antlered and hauling a sleigh: one of Santa's reindeer.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who performs rhythmic dancing in metal-soled shoes is a stage performer, a kind of entertainer.

clue.text: After exercise, the lifting of roast ducks is child’s play

indicators.note: in a down entry, lifting something raises it so it reads from bottom to top

blocks.note: PE is physical education, school exercise
to roast is to cook in an oven
a duck is a score of nought, and O looks like zero

explanation.surface: After a workout, hoisting the roast ducks out of the oven is easy work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Child's play' means something easy, but here it is literal: a game for babies. In cricket a duck is a score of zero.
explanation.definitionFit: This hide-and-reveal game, where a face is covered then shown, is played with babies and toddlers.

clue.text: Record books sure to include Apple’s core corporate symbols

indicators.note: to include something is to take it inside, so one piece holds another
the core of something is its centre, so the middle letter is kept

blocks.note: a log is a written record
OT is the Old Testament, a set of books of the Bible
'sure!' is an informal yes
the middle letter of the fruit

explanation.surface: A record label's catalogue is certain to feature the tech giant's main brand marks.
explanation.walkthrough: Apple suggests the computer company, but only the centre of the word is used. OT, the Old Testament, is a common crossword abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: A logotype is a company's distinctive emblem or wordmark, so several of them are trademark designs.

clue.text: Matches involving ‘The Greatest Footballers’

indicators.note: to involve something is to take it in, so one piece sits inside another

blocks.note: a tie that goes with a shirt matches it
boxer Muhammad Ali called himself The Greatest

explanation.surface: A list of fixtures featuring the finest players.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Matches' looks like a noun for games, but it is a verb; The Greatest is Ali's own nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: Goalkeepers are members of a football team, so they are a particular kind of player of the game.

clue.text: Part of the body below nuts

indicators.note: nuts means crazy, and crazy letters fall out of order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A rude anatomical reference to what lies beneath the testicles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nuts' invites the slang reading, but it is a signal that the word before it is jumbled.
explanation.definitionFit: The elbow is the joint in the middle of the arm, one anatomical section of a person.

clue.text: Look after Polish and American cattle

indicators.note: coming after something means following it, so the word before this one is placed at the end

blocks.note: to buff is to polish to a shine
A is a standard abbreviation for American
lo, as in 'lo and behold', means look

explanation.surface: Someone minding Polish and American cows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Look after' reads as 'tend', but 'after' simply places the look word last. Polish is not the nationality but the verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Buffalo are large wild or domesticated bovines, so they belong to the same family as cows and oxen.

clue.text: Old lady that’s two thousand and one?!

blocks.note: a grand is slang for a thousand, and M is the Roman numeral for another thousand
a means one

explanation.surface: An elderly woman likened to the year 2001.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'two thousand' is two separate thousands, one slang and one Roman; 'and' is part of the reading, joining them.
explanation.definitionFit: A grandmother is often affectionately called an old lady, informally meaning an elderly female relative.

clue.text: Belief in God arising seconds from impending fatality

indicators.note: in a down entry, something arising goes up, so it reads from bottom to top
the second letter of each following word is kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the second letter of each word

explanation.surface: Faith springing up as death approaches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Belief in God' reads as one phrase, but the definition is just the first word and 'God' is the fodder turned upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A dogma is a firmly held doctrine or tenet, an article of faith laid down as true.

clue.text: Vehicle reversing skirts loud F1 cars

indicators.note: something reversing goes backwards, so the letters run the other way
to skirt something is to go round its edges, so one piece surrounds another

blocks.note: a cart is a wheeled vehicle
f is forte, the musical direction for loud
F as written, and 1 looks like I

explanation.surface: A car backing round the edge of a track full of noisy Formula One racers.
explanation.walkthrough: F1 suggests motor racing, but it is read as letter F and the digit standing for I.
explanation.definitionFit: Traffic is the collective term for vehicles moving on roads, so it stands for cars en masse.

clue.text: Spike Milligan’s behind superhero movie put on

indicators.note: a behind is the rear end, so the last letter is taken

blocks.note: the Marvel film about the Norse god of thunder
final letter

explanation.surface: The comedian Spike Milligan's backside appearing in a superhero film.
explanation.walkthrough: Spike Milligan was a British comic of The Goon Show; here his first name is the definition and his surname gives a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A thorn is a sharp pointed growth on a plant stem, so it is a natural prickle.

clue.text: Queen Elizabeth abandoning walled city where jewels are kept?

indicators.note: abandoning something leaves it behind, so those letters are dropped

blocks.note: Elizabeth Regina, the royal cipher
Chester is an English city famous for its Roman and medieval walls

explanation.surface: The monarch leaving a fortified city where treasure is stored.
explanation.walkthrough: The royal ER is taken from the end of the city's name. The question mark admits a box is only one place gems are stored.
explanation.definitionFit: A chest is a sturdy lidded box, the classic place for storing treasure such as gems.

clue.text: Bag or other container containing hot shelled egg

indicators.note: a box containing goods holds them inside, so one piece goes within another
shelling removes the outer case, so only the inner letter remains

blocks.note: a tin is a metal container
H is the tap abbreviation for hot
the middle letter

explanation.surface: A bag or another receptacle holding a hot peeled egg.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bag' looks like a container listed beside 'other container', but it is the slang sense: something you are into, as in 'not my bag'.
explanation.definitionFit: Saying 'it's my bag' or 'it's my thing' both mean a personal interest or preferred pursuit.

clue.text: Hot, welcoming brown drink drunk by cold European?

indicators.note: to welcome someone is to take them in, so one piece goes inside another
what is drunk goes inside the drinker, so this piece is enclosed

blocks.note: C is the tap abbreviation for cold
taken as written
a fizzy soft drink
E is the abbreviation for European

explanation.surface: A warm cocoa being drunk by a chilly continental traveller.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface invites 'hot drink' as the definition, but HOT and the cola are wordplay; the definition is the colour word, a deep brown.
explanation.definitionFit: Chocolate is the name of a dark reddish-brown shade, named after the confectionery.

clue.text: Where exhausted runner eats tuna melts?

definitions.text: Where exhausted runner eats tuna melts?
definitions.note: the whole clue is the definition

indicators.note: something exhausted is emptied out, so only the outer letters remain
melting things lose their shape and run together into a new form

blocks.note: the first and last letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: A worn-out jogger refuels on toasted tuna-and-cheese sandwiches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tuna melts' looks like a dish, but 'melts' is the verb signalling the mix. The whole clue also describes where a tired athlete might dine.
explanation.definitionFit: A place where meals are served to paying customers is just where a hungry athlete might order a toasted sandwich.

clue.text: Unopened squash, say, left on the QE2

indicators.note: something unopened has not had its front opened, so the first letter is missing

blocks.note: squash is an example of a racket game

explanation.surface: A sealed bottle of fruit drink forgotten aboard the famous Cunard liner.
explanation.walkthrough: Squash is a fruit cordial in Britain, but here it is the racket game; 'say' marks it as an example. The QE2 was a Cunard ocean liner.
explanation.definitionFit: On ships the left-hand side facing forward is called by this nautical term, so it fits any vessel including that liner.
